skills.title: iOS Development
skills.description: Build, inspect, repair, analyze, package, and optionally install native Objective-C and C iOS applications directly on an iOS device using the locally installed Altivec Toolchain, an installed iPhoneOS SDK, managed Altivec static libraries, UIKit, Make, `.app` bundles, and IPA archives. Use this skill for legacy or jailbroken-device iOS development and for portable C code shared with Cocoa applications.
skills.instructions:
## Operating Principles

Inspect the project before changing it. Read every applicable `AGENTS.md`, the
existing Makefile, `Info.plist`, nearby source, and relevant tests or harnesses.
Preserve established project conventions unless the user explicitly asks to
change them. Assume any compilation and file changes are happening locally on the device, yes even on iPhones.

Make small, focused changes. Preserve unrelated work. Never commit or push.
Do not install an app, restart a process, delete user data, or alter system
packages unless the user explicitly asks.

## Environment Discovery

Before designing or changing a build, inspect the local environment with
read-only commands such as:

```sh
uname -a
uname -m
id
pwd
command -v clang
command -v make
command -v altivec-sdk
command -v altivec-lib
command -v ldid
command -v zip
test -f /var/altivec/share/altivec/make/ios-app.mk
test -f /var/altivec/share/altivec/templates/ios-app/Makefile
altivec-sdk list
altivec-lib list
```

Also inspect the project rather than assuming a template layout:

```sh
find . -name AGENTS.md -print
sed -n '1,240p' Makefile
sed -n '1,240p' Info.plist
ls -la
for directory in source/shared source/iOS source/macOS source/linux; do
  test ! -d "$directory" || find "$directory" -type f -print
done
```

Keep discovery bounded to the project and known toolchain roots. Do not perform
an unbounded scan of the entire device. Treat command presence as evidence only
that a command exists; confirm its version and supported targets before relying
on it.

## SDK Configuration

Use only the SDKs and developer tools installed by the user through the
`AltivecToolchain` Debian package and `altivec-sdk`. The canonical toolchain
prefix is `/var/altivec`; iOS may resolve `/var` through `/private/var`, but
project files must use the canonical `/var/altivec` spelling.

First verify the SDK build components:

```sh
command -v clang
command -v altivec-sdk
test -f /var/altivec/share/altivec/make/ios-app.mk
```

If any check fails, stop and ask the user to install or repair the
`AltivecToolchain` Debian package. Do not clone Altivec Intelligence, download a
replacement compiler, invent a compatible path, or modify system directories.

Run `altivec-sdk list` to identify installed, selected, and device-compatible
SDKs. The coding agent is not root. It may list SDKs, but it cannot install,
select, or verify them: those three commands require root and write under
`/var/altivec`, `/var/lib/altivec-sdk`, or `/var/cache/altivec-sdk`.

If the required SDK is missing, incompatible, unselected, or needs privileged
verification, ask the user to perform the appropriate operation. Give the user
the exact command only after identifying the required version, for example:

```sh
altivec-sdk install 8.4
altivec-sdk select 8.4
altivec-sdk verify 8.4
```

Do not run these privileged commands yourself. Do not use `sudo`, assume a root
password, download SDK archives manually, copy an SDK from another system, or
commit SDK contents. After the user acts, rerun `altivec-sdk list` and the build
preflight.

Treat SDK version and deployment target as separate settings. The SDK controls
the headers and linker inputs available at build time; the deployment target
controls the oldest supported runtime. Keep `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` and
the `MinimumOSVersion` value in `Info.plist` consistent. Never lower the runtime
floor merely to silence a build error.

By default, make new applications use the iPhoneOS8.4 SDK with a minimum
deployment target of iOS 4.3. These old systems lack NSJSONSerialization as well
as networking that supports modern TLS so rely on AltivecCocoa which is described later to provide this functionality even on iOS 4.3.

## Managed Altivec Libraries

Use `altivec-lib` for application-facing Altivec static libraries. It installs
AltivecCore and AltivecCocoa together as one versioned set because Cocoa builds
on Core. Do not download release ZIPs manually, copy individual archives into a
project, or mix Core and Cocoa versions.

First confirm that both the manager and its Make integration are installed:

```sh
command -v altivec-lib
test -f /var/altivec/share/altivec/make/ios-app.mk
```

If either check fails, stop and ask the user to install or repair the
`AltivecToolchain` Debian package.

`altivec-lib list` is read-only and shows every local version plus the selected
version. The coding agent may run it during discovery. Installing, updating,
selecting, and verifying libraries are privileged operations that write under
`/var/altivec`, `/var/lib/altivec-lib`, or `/var/cache/altivec-lib`. When user
action is required, provide the exact applicable command:

```sh
# Install an exact release. Omit the leading "v" from the Git tag.
altivec-lib install 1.0.9

# Install and select the latest stable release, but never downgrade.
altivec-lib update

# Roll back to an already installed version.
altivec-lib select 1.0.9

# Recheck an installed version against the selected SDK.
altivec-lib verify 1.0.9
```

Do not run those privileged commands without permission. After the user acts,
rerun `altivec-lib list`. A usable selection has a relative
`/var/altivec/Libraries/Current` symlink and a generated
`/var/altivec/share/altivec-lib/current.mk`. Do not edit either one by hand.
Older installed versions remain available for explicit rollback.

The managed pair supplies the modern C foundation needed by legacy Cocoa
applications. `libAltivecCore.a` aggregates libcurl, SQLite, cJSON, and their
required static dependencies; AltivecCocoa adds the UIKit/Cocoa-facing classes
and Font Awesome support. Together they let an iOS 4.3 application perform
modern HTTP/HTTPS networking, structured JSON processing, and SQLite storage
without depending on obsolete system copies of those libraries. Continue to
use APIs compatible with the deployment target, set network timeouts, and keep
TLS peer and host verification enabled.

## Architecture and Deployment Target

Build only for the architecture of the device on which the coding agent is
running. Determine it from `uname -m`, confirm the compiler target support, and
read the usable-target column from `altivec-sdk list`. Do not create a fat
ARMv7/ARM64 binary on-device and do not build an architecture merely because
the SDK contains its headers.

Let the installed common rules select their supported native architecture.
Never override `ALTIVEC_ARCH`, a target triple, or `-arch` until the compiler,
linker, SDK, and device have all been confirmed to support the same value. If
the installed package cannot build the device's architecture, report the exact
mismatch and ask the user for a compatible toolchain package.

Choose the deployment target from the existing project requirement and actual
device support. Before using an API newer than that target, either use an
established compatibility wrapper with a safe runtime fallback or ask the user
to raise the target. A newer SDK does not make a newer symbol safe on an older
runtime.

## Project Structure

For a new cross-platform Cocoa application, prefer a source tree such as:

```text
MyApp/
  AGENTS.md                         optional project-specific guidance
  source/
    shared/                         code and resources used by both targets
      app_model.h
      app_model.c                   portable business logic
      Resources/
        en.lproj/
          Localizable.strings
    iOS/
      Makefile                      run iOS make commands from this directory
      Info.plist
      main.m
      AppDelegate.h
      AppDelegate.m
      UI/                           UIKit controllers and views
      Bridge/                       iOS Objective-C/C adapters
      Resources/
        AppIcon.png
      build-release/                generated MyApp.app and MyApp.ipa
      build-analyze/                generated Clang analyzer report
    macOS/                          optional sibling desktop target
      Makefile
      Info.plist
      UI/
      Bridge/
      Resources/
      build-release/                generated macOS app bundle
      build-analyze/                generated Clang analyzer report
```

Keep UIKit code in the platform UI layer. Keep networking policy, parsing,
database work, computation, and reusable business logic in portable C when
practical. Use a small, named bridge layer to convert between Cocoa objects and
C types. Put only genuinely cross-platform files under `source/shared`; never
put UIKit or AppKit imports in ordinary shared C files. Do not move an existing
project merely to match this example.

Keep generated output beside the Makefile that owns it. With the layout above,
the iOS release paths are `source/iOS/build-release/MyApp.app` and
`source/iOS/build-release/MyApp.ipa`. Do not create a shared
`source/build-release` directory unless the existing top-level build system
explicitly owns that path. Keep all build and analyzer directories ignored by
version control.

## Makefile Configuration

Place the iOS Makefile in `source/iOS` and run its commands from that directory.
Resolve `../shared` relative to that location. Reuse an existing Makefile when
present. For a new project, change to `source/iOS` and copy the installed
template rather than reconstructing the Altivec rules:

```sh
cp /var/altivec/share/altivec/templates/ios-app/Makefile ./Makefile
```

Do not overwrite an existing Makefile. Edit only the project declarations
above the common include. A representative Makefile is:

```makefile
APP_NAME := MyApp

SOURCES := \
	main.m \
	AppDelegate.m \
	UI/MainViewController.m \
	../shared/app_model.c \
	Bridge/AppModelBridge.m

RESOURCES := \
	AppIcon.png

# Make bridge imports of app_model.h resolve without exposing UIKit to C.
INCLUDE_DIRS := ../shared

# Foundation, UIKit, and CoreGraphics are automatic. Add only dependencies.
FRAMEWORKS := Security

# Keep warnings enabled for C and Objective-C and make zero warnings binding.
APP_CFLAGS := -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror
APP_OBJCFLAGS := -Wobjc-method-access -Wundeclared-selector

# Select one memory-management model for Objective-C files in this target.
# Use 0 for MRC projects or shared legacy Objective-C; use 1 only when the
# inspected deployment target and all Objective-C sources support ARC.
APP_USE_ARC := 0

include /var/altivec/share/altivec/make/ios-app.mk
```

When `altivec-lib` has a selected version, leave `ALTIVEC_LIBS` unset. The
common rules automatically include the generated selection fragment, add the
managed Core and Cocoa header paths, link `libAltivecCocoa.a` before
`libAltivecCore.a`, and add CoreText. Do not repeat those paths or archives in
`INCLUDE_DIRS`, `APP_LDFLAGS`, or `APP_LDLIBS`, and do not add a second copy of
CoreText to `FRAMEWORKS` merely because AltivecCocoa uses it.

When migrating an older project, remove any manual Altivec include paths,
individual Core component archives, `libAltivecCore.a`, and
`libAltivecCocoa.a` entries before relying on the automatic integration.
Otherwise the same objects may be linked twice or in an untested order.

For a project that intentionally must not use the selected libraries, place the
opt-out before the common include:

```makefile
ALTIVEC_LIBS := none
```

Do not use the opt-out to conceal missing or corrupt managed libraries. A build
that needs Altivec APIs must fail clearly until the selected version verifies.
During a managed build, the link output reports `[LIBS] Altivec VERSION`.

The installed iOS rules use one `RESOURCE_ROOT` (normally `Resources`) and
require every `RESOURCES` entry to be a safe relative path beneath it. Never
list `../shared/Resources` as a resource entry. If localized strings or other
assets live under `source/shared/Resources`, reuse or add a project-owned copy
or staging hook that places them at the iOS app-bundle root before IPA
packaging. If the build has no such hook, keep a package-ready copy under
`source/iOS/Resources`. Do not assume shared resources are bundled merely
because shared source files compile.

The common rules also copy the selected libraries' managed bundle resources
before copying project resources. This automatically stages `cacert.pem`, Font
Awesome OTF files, their license notice, and any other resources shipped in the
supported static-package layout. Project `RESOURCES` deliberately win when the
same destination exists. Treat an override of `cacert.pem` or a managed font as
an explicit compatibility decision; an accidental replacement can break TLS or
font loading. Managed resource staging is reported as
`[RESOURCES] Altivec VERSION`.

Adjust names, sources, resources, frameworks, language standard, and ARC only
from evidence in the project. Do not copy the sample mechanically. Keep
`-Wall` enabled whether the selected compiler is GCC-compatible or Clang. Add
`-Wextra` and relevant language warnings when supported. Fix every warning; do
not hide warnings globally or remove useful warning flags to obtain a green
build. If an old API is intentionally required, isolate any narrowly scoped
deprecation suppression inside the compatibility implementation and document
the runtime fallback.

Every project Makefile must provide at least these public commands:

```sh
make release
make clean
make analyze
```

The installed iOS application rules already provide `release`, `analyze`, and
`clean`. `make release` must create a signed `.app` and a correctly structured
IPA. `make clean` must remove only generated build and analysis directories;
it must never remove sources, resources, SDKs, or user data.

## Application Bundle and Package Structure

An iOS application bundle has a flat root. A normal release output resembles:

```text
build-release/
  MyApp.app/
    MyApp                    Mach-O executable for this device architecture
    Info.plist
    PkgInfo                  optional legacy metadata
    AppIcon.png              example resource
    en.lproj/
      Localizable.strings
    Frameworks/              only when the deployment target permits embedding
    _CodeSignature/          present only when produced by the signing flow
  MyApp.ipa
```

An IPA is a ZIP archive whose root contains `Payload`, not another project or
build directory:

```text
MyApp.ipa
  Payload/
    MyApp.app/
      MyApp
      Info.plist
      PkgInfo
      AppIcon.png
      en.lproj/
        Localizable.strings
```

Keep `CFBundleExecutable` equal to the executable name. Preserve resource
subdirectories. Do not place macOS-style `Contents/MacOS` or
`Contents/Resources` directories inside an iOS `.app`. Do not call a bare app
directory an IPA; the IPA must be a valid ZIP archive with the `Payload`
layout.

Prefer static C-library linkage for legacy iOS targets. Embedded dynamic iOS
frameworks require runtime support that older systems may not provide. Never
copy a dynamic framework into the bundle without confirming the deployment
target, architectures, install names, code signing, and loader behavior.

## Info.plist and Resources

Require a project-owned `Info.plist`. At minimum, verify coherent values for:

- `CFBundleExecutable`
- `CFBundleIdentifier`
- `CFBundleName` or `CFBundleDisplayName`
- `CFBundlePackageType` (`APPL`)
- `CFBundleShortVersionString`
- `CFBundleVersion`
- `LSRequiresIPhoneOS`
- `MinimumOSVersion`

Add only capability, orientation, background-mode, URL-scheme, privacy, or
device-family keys the application actually needs. Do not fabricate signing
identities, entitlements, bundle identifiers, version numbers, or privacy
usage descriptions. Ask the user when those values are product decisions.

List resources relative to `Resources/` when using the installed common rules.
Keep their relative paths in the app bundle. Never list `Info.plist`, the app
executable, an absolute path, or a path containing `..` as a resource. Verify
that every listed resource exists before building.

Keep iOS-only icons, launch images, and other UIKit presentation assets under
`source/iOS/Resources`. Reference icon filenames with the `Info.plist` keys
supported by the selected SDK and deployment target. Do not introduce an asset
catalog unless an installed `actool` workflow already supports it; the local
Altivec Make rules package ordinary files and do not imply Xcode asset-catalog
compilation.

Store localized resources in language-specific directories such as:

```text
Resources/
  en.lproj/
    Localizable.strings
    InfoPlist.strings        optional localized bundle metadata
  ja.lproj/
    Localizable.strings
    InfoPlist.strings
```

Copy each `.lproj` directory intact to the root of the iOS `.app`. Use
`NSLocalizedString` or the project's established localization API instead of
hard-coded user-facing strings. Preserve the encoding required by the target
runtime and validate that every supported locale contains the required keys.
Keep common JSON, HTML, fonts, certificates, and other runtime data under
`source/shared/Resources` only when both platform Makefiles explicitly stage
them.

## Launch Screens and Launch Images

Launch configuration and application layout are separate responsibilities. A
correct launch asset lets UIKit start the application in the intended full-screen
geometry instead of a compatibility-sized or letterboxed canvas. It does not
make the application's views adaptive. The real first view must still handle
every supported size, orientation, status-bar height, safe area, camera housing,
and home-indicator inset through the project's compatibility layer.

Inspect `MinimumOSVersion`, `UISupportedInterfaceOrientations`, existing launch
keys, and available build tools before choosing a launch mechanism. Use this
order of preference:

1. Keep the canonical static PNGs required by the iOS 4.3 through iOS 7 portion
   of a legacy deployment range.
2. For newer systems, prefer one simple compiled launch storyboard when the
   installed build has a proven `ibtool` rule. A launch storyboard adapts to new
   screen sizes without a new full-screen bitmap for every phone.
3. When the on-device build cannot compile a launch storyboard, use explicit
   `UILaunchImages` entries and the static matrix below for every device family
   the user actually supports and tests.

Do not merely copy `LaunchScreen.storyboard` into `RESOURCES`. UIKit needs the
compiled storyboard product, and the installed common Make rules do not imply
that `ibtool` or asset-catalog compilation exists. Do not add
`UILaunchStoryboardName` until the compiled resource is present in the final
application and has been tested on both the oldest and newest target systems.
Static images remain necessary for iOS versions that predate launch
storyboards.

Design the launch screen as a static approximation of the first application
frame, not as an advertisement, progress screen, login state, or versioned
splash page. Use a full-bleed background and keep logos or other meaningful
content near the center so cropping, rounded corners, the iPhone X sensor
housing, and later display features cannot obscure it. Do not bake a status bar
or device chrome into the bitmap. Generate opaque, sRGB PNG files with exact,
case-sensitive names and dimensions.

### Static portrait matrix

For the legacy-through-X-era static fallback, create these files directly under
`source/iOS/Resources`. Dimensions are full portrait canvases:

| iPhone family                      |   UIKit size | Scale |  PNG pixels | Required filename           |
| ---------------------------------- | -----------: | ----: | ----------: | --------------------------- |
| 3GS and earlier 3.5-inch           | 320 x 480 pt |    1x |   320 x 480 | `Default.png`               |
| 4 and 4S                           | 320 x 480 pt |    2x |   640 x 960 | `Default@2x.png`            |
| 5, 5c, 5s, and first-generation SE | 320 x 568 pt |    2x |  640 x 1136 | `Default-568h@2x.png`       |
| 6, 6s, 7, 8, and 4.7-inch SE       | 375 x 667 pt |    2x |  750 x 1334 | `Default-iOS8-667h@2x.png`  |
| 6/6s/7/8 Plus                      | 414 x 736 pt |    3x | 1242 x 2208 | `Default-iOS8-736h@3x.png`  |
| X, XS, and 11 Pro                  | 375 x 812 pt |    3x | 1125 x 2436 | `Default-iOS11-812h@3x.png` |
| XR and 11                          | 414 x 896 pt |    2x |  828 x 1792 | `Default-iOS12-896h@2x.png` |
| XS Max and 11 Pro Max              | 414 x 896 pt |    3x | 1242 x 2688 | `Default-iOS12-896h@3x.png` |

The Plus-family launch canvas is the 3x UIKit render size, 1242 x 2208, even
though those devices downsample to a 1080 x 1920 physical panel. Do not replace
it with the physical panel dimensions. Likewise, do not infer future launch
assets solely from marketing display pixels: UIKit point size, UIKit scale, and
native scale can differ.

The first three filenames are compatibility conventions used by older iOS
versions. The later names are explicit project conventions and must match the
`UILaunchImages` dictionaries below. `UILaunchImageName` contains the base name
without `.png`, `@2x`, `@3x`, or the legacy `-568h` modifier. Both 414 x 896
files intentionally share one base name so UIKit can select the correct scale.

### Generating the PNG files with ImageMagick

Use a reviewed, high-resolution master whose critical content is safe under a
center crop. Never stretch one aspect ratio into another. The following commands
make an opaque, centered cover crop for each required canvas:

```sh
master="LaunchScreenMaster.png"
test -f "$master"
mkdir -p Resources

make_launch_image() {
  width="$1"
  height="$2"
  output="$3"
  magick "$master" \
    -colorspace sRGB \
    -filter Lanczos \
    -resize "${width}x${height}^" \
    -gravity center \
    -extent "${width}x${height}" \
    -background '#ffffff' \
    -alpha remove \
    -alpha off \
    -strip \
    "PNG24:Resources/${output}"
}

make_launch_image 320 480 Default.png
make_launch_image 640 960 Default@2x.png
make_launch_image 640 1136 Default-568h@2x.png
make_launch_image 750 1334 Default-iOS8-667h@2x.png
make_launch_image 1242 2208 Default-iOS8-736h@3x.png
make_launch_image 1125 2436 Default-iOS11-812h@3x.png
make_launch_image 828 1792 Default-iOS12-896h@2x.png
make_launch_image 1242 2688 Default-iOS12-896h@3x.png
```

If centered cropping would remove meaningful artwork, stop and redesign the
master as separable background and centered foreground layers instead of
distorting or blindly cropping it. Do not generate launch images from an app
icon by stretching it to full-screen size.

Verify dimensions and color channels before editing the Makefile:

```sh
magick identify -format '%f %wx%h %[channels]\n' \
  Resources/Default*.png
```

### Info.plist launch selection

Keep `UILaunchImageFile` for pre-iOS 7 naming and add an explicit
`UILaunchImages` array for iOS 7 and later. A portrait application supporting
the matrix above uses:

```xml
<key>UILaunchImageFile</key>
<string>Default</string>
<key>UILaunchImages</key>
<array>
  <dict>
    <key>UILaunchImageMinimumOSVersion</key>
    <string>7.0</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageName</key>
    <string>Default</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageOrientation</key>
    <string>Portrait</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageSize</key>
    <string>{320, 480}</string>
  </dict>
  <dict>
    <key>UILaunchImageMinimumOSVersion</key>
    <string>7.0</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageName</key>
    <string>Default</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageOrientation</key>
    <string>Portrait</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageSize</key>
    <string>{320, 568}</string>
  </dict>
  <dict>
    <key>UILaunchImageMinimumOSVersion</key>
    <string>8.0</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageName</key>
    <string>Default-iOS8-667h</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageOrientation</key>
    <string>Portrait</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageSize</key>
    <string>{375, 667}</string>
  </dict>
  <dict>
    <key>UILaunchImageMinimumOSVersion</key>
    <string>8.0</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageName</key>
    <string>Default-iOS8-736h</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageOrientation</key>
    <string>Portrait</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageSize</key>
    <string>{414, 736}</string>
  </dict>
  <dict>
    <key>UILaunchImageMinimumOSVersion</key>
    <string>11.0</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageName</key>
    <string>Default-iOS11-812h</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageOrientation</key>
    <string>Portrait</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageSize</key>
    <string>{375, 812}</string>
  </dict>
  <dict>
    <key>UILaunchImageMinimumOSVersion</key>
    <string>12.0</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageName</key>
    <string>Default-iOS12-896h</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageOrientation</key>
    <string>Portrait</string>
    <key>UILaunchImageSize</key>
    <string>{414, 896}</string>
  </dict>
</array>
```

When `UILaunchImages` exists, iOS 7 and later use it instead of falling back to
old filename discovery, so do not omit the 320 x 480 or 320 x 568 entries. Each
dictionary's size is in portrait points even when an application launches in
landscape. For a landscape-only iPhone application, keep the bitmap height
greater than its width and rotate the artwork inside that portrait-sized canvas;
then follow the project's tested orientation configuration rather than creating
arbitrary landscape pixel dimensions.

List every PNG at the top level of `RESOURCES` before the common Make include so
the files land at the root of the `.app`, where UIKit requires launch images:

```makefile
RESOURCES += \
	Default.png \
	Default@2x.png \
	Default-568h@2x.png \
	Default-iOS8-667h@2x.png \
	Default-iOS8-736h@3x.png \
	Default-iOS11-812h@3x.png \
	Default-iOS12-896h@2x.png \
	Default-iOS12-896h@3x.png
```

For iPhone 12 and later, use a compiled launch storyboard whenever possible.
Static full-screen PNG enumeration is not future-proof. If the user explicitly
requires a post-X static fallback and no storyboard compiler is available,
consult Apple's current device-dimension table, add one uniquely named file and
one `UILaunchImages` dictionary for every distinct UIKit point-size and scale,
and test each requested device family. Never claim that an iPhone X image alone
provides native full-screen launch behavior on all later phones.

After building, verify all declared launch files at the application-bundle root
and inspect the packaged plist. Test at least the oldest device, every distinct
screen geometry the user requested, and the newest device. A successful launch
on one Retina phone is not evidence that the other launch entries work. Remember
that iOS can cache launch snapshots; reinstall the development build when a
known-new launch image does not appear, but do not erase application data unless
the user approved that consequence.

Primary references are Apple's
[Information Property List key reference](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/General/Reference/InfoPlistKeyReference/Articles/iPhoneOSKeys.html),
[legacy landscape launch-image note](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/technotes/tn2244/_index.html),
[iPhone Plus render-scale explanation](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/qa/qa1909/),
and current [device layout specifications](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout).

## Coding Style

Never use Swift. Write Objective-C for Cocoa/UI integration and C for portable
logic. Use bracketed Objective-C message syntax. Do not use dot syntax, even for
properties:

```objective-c
[[controller view] setHidden:NO];
title = [item title];
```

Do not write:

```objective-c
controller.view.hidden = NO;
title = item.title;
```

Match the existing indentation and naming conventions. In a new project,
prefer 2-space indentation, no tabs in source, readable lower-camel-case
method names, trailing underscores for private instance variables, and
prefixed public C symbols. Use `YES` and `NO` for `BOOL`. Do not compare a
`BOOL` directly with `YES` merely to test truth.

Avoid premature optimization, but prefer pure C for hot computation, parsers,
database adapters, and reusable business rules when it gives a clear
portability or performance benefit. Also prefer C when working with C libraries such as libcurl, SQLite, and cJSON. Keep UI lifecycle, view construction,
event handling, and conversion to display objects in Objective-C.

## C and Objective-C Boundaries

Keep ordinary `.c` files platform-neutral. Do not include UIKit, Foundation,
CoreFoundation, Objective-C runtime, or other Apple-framework headers from C.
Use standard C headers and project-owned portable headers. Do not make a C
header expose `NSString`, `NSArray`, `NSData`, Objective-C `id`, or UIKit types.

Do not let every Objective-C file import the C model and third-party C
libraries. Designate narrow bridge `.m` files that are allowed to include both
sides. Expose Objective-C methods to the UI and portable C functions to the C
core. Convert strings, byte buffers, ownership, errors, and callbacks at that
boundary.

Objective-C may include narrow system C headers when Cocoa has no suitable
surface, but keep those uses local. Import project C headers, `curl/curl.h`,
`sqlite3.h`, and `cJSON.h` only in designated model or bridge implementations.
Never pass a `cJSON *`, `sqlite3 *`, or libcurl handle into a view controller.

Keep C libraries in C as long as possible. Parse network responses, execute SQL,
and transform cJSON trees in C. Bridge only the final model or presentation data
needed by UIKit. Make ownership rules explicit on both sides of every bridge.

## Memory Management and Runtime Compatibility

For ARC code, do not add manual ownership messages. Remember that zeroing
`weak` is unavailable before iOS 5. Use an established `assign` or
`__unsafe_unretained` back-pointer only when the deployment floor requires it,
and document the lifetime invariant.

Prefer delegate methods, selectors, or C callback functions for shared
compatibility code. Use properties, class extensions, object literals,
subscripting, `instancetype`, and other newer Objective-C features only after
confirming the compiler, SDK, runtime floor, and project style all support them.
Dot syntax remains forbidden even when a property is valid.

Put SDK-version and platform compatibility logic in a small compatibility
layer, commonly named `XPFoundation` or `XPUIKit`. At feature call sites, call
the wrapper rather than repeating `#if` checks. For a selector absent from the
oldest runtime, first test `respondsToSelector:` and invoke it through an
appropriately typed, project-approved bridge; provide an oldest-runtime
fallback. Use compile-time checks for declarations the compiler must parse and
runtime checks for symbols that may or may not exist on the device.

## AltivecToolchain

Use the installed Altivec Toolchain as the source of the on-device compiler,
linker, SDK and library managers, signing utility, Make rules, and modern C
development artifacts. Do not confuse a command-line program with a linkable
application library: the presence of `curl` or `sqlite3` on `PATH` does not
prove that a managed Altivec library version is installed and selected. Use
`altivec-lib list` as the source of truth.

The manager normalizes each selected release under a layout like:

```text
/var/altivec/Libraries/1.0.9/
  AltivecCore/
    include/
    lib/libAltivecCore.a
    lib/cacert.pem
  AltivecCocoa/
    include/
    lib/libAltivecCocoa.a
    Resources/
  Bundle/
    cacert.pem
    Fonts/
```

Applications may import the public umbrella headers when the selected release
provides them:

```objective-c
#import <AltivecCore/AltivecCore.h>
#import <AltivecCocoa/AltivecCocoa.h>
```

Include third-party headers such as `curl/curl.h`, `sqlite3.h`, and `cJSON.h`
only in the narrow C or Objective-C bridge implementations that own those APIs.
Do not refer to a concrete version directory or the `Current` symlink from a
project Makefile. The generated `current.mk` deliberately pins each invocation
to the selected version's real paths and owns static link order.

Never embed `AltivecCore.framework` or `AltivecCocoa.framework` in an application
targeting iOS 4.3 through iOS 7. The managed iOS releases are static precisely
because those runtimes do not support the modern embedded-framework model.
Never manually add the component archives behind `libAltivecCore.a`; doing so
can duplicate symbols and defeat the aggregate library's tested dependency
order.

If a required header, archive, CA bundle, font, or generated selection fragment
is absent, stop and ask the user to install, update, select, or verify the
managed version. Do not download, compile, or install a replacement into a
system directory. Never disable TLS peer or host verification to make a request
succeed.

## Third-Party Libraries

Keep libcurl operations, header callbacks, response buffers, and error mapping
in a C networking module. Keep SQLite connections, statements, transactions,
and row decoding in a C storage module. Keep cJSON parsing and serialization in
C model or protocol modules. Expose narrow application-specific functions
rather than raw third-party handles.

Check every return code. Bound network and parser inputs. Use prepared SQLite
statements and bind values rather than concatenating untrusted SQL. Finalize
statements, close handles, free cJSON trees, and release all allocated buffers
on every success and error path. Set libcurl timeouts and preserve TLS
verification.

Use `altivec-lib verify VERSION` to confirm the architecture and linkability of
managed Altivec archives. For project-owned third-party archives, independently
confirm that each one contains the target device architecture. Do not link a
host, simulator, macOS, or wrong-architecture archive. Do not mix headers from
one installation with a library from another prefix. Record any required
license or attribution resource in the app bundle when the dependency requires
it; the manager already stages the Font Awesome notice shipped with
AltivecCocoa.

## Build, Analysis, and Verification

After source or build changes, run a clean analysis and release build while
capturing the complete output:

```sh
make clean
make analyze
make release
```

Do not truncate output with `tail`. Keep any temporary log outside committed
resources and do not commit generated logs, apps, IPAs, analyzer reports,
objects, or dependency files unless the user explicitly asks.

Require zero compiler warnings and zero analyzer diagnostics. An empty
`build-analyze/analyze.txt` may mean the analysis is clean; confirm the command
completed and the report covered the expected sources. Do not claim analysis
ran when Clang or the target rule was unavailable.

Verify outputs with available local tools:

```sh
test -d build-release/MyApp.app
test -f build-release/MyApp.ipa
file build-release/MyApp.app/MyApp
otool -hv build-release/MyApp.app/MyApp
unzip -l build-release/MyApp.ipa
```

Replace `MyApp` with the actual `APP_NAME`. Confirm the Mach-O architecture
matches the device, the IPA contains `Payload/MyApp.app`, the executable and
`Info.plist` are present, and all required resources were copied. Inspect
linkage and signing with the locally available `otool` and `ldid` commands when
relevant. If the environment supports running the app, treat a launch without
an exception or missing-selector crash as additional verification, never as a
replacement for a clean build.

## Installation and Execution

Building an IPA does not authorize installing or launching it. Install only
when the user asks, and first confirm the exact IPA path and bundle identifier.

When `appinst` is available, prefer:

```sh
appinst build-release/MyApp.ipa
```

Otherwise, when `ipainstaller` is available, use:

```sh
ipainstaller build-release/MyApp.ipa
```

Choose one installer before starting. Do not automatically try another after a
failure because the first may have partially changed device state. Do not use
`ipainstaller -c` unless the user requests a clean installation because it can
erase the application's documents and resources. Do not use `-f` unless the
user explicitly accepts bypassing compatibility checks. Do not use `-d`
because it deletes the IPA. The `-i` option displays installed-app information;
it is not the install operation.

### Launching Applications with Activator

Treat installing and launching as separate device mutations. Launch an
application after installation only when the user asked to install and run,
launch, open, or test it. An install-only request does not authorize launching
the application.

Prefer Activator's command-line interface for post-install launching. Do not
link `libactivator` into an ordinary application merely to launch that
application from the development shell. First verify that Activator is
installed:

```sh
command -v activator
```

If it is missing, ask the user to install the `libactivator` package. Do not
attempt to install it or another system package without permission.

Obtain the exact, case-sensitive `CFBundleIdentifier` from the built
application's `Info.plist`. Do not derive it from the application name,
executable name, Debian package identifier, or IPA filename. When `plistutil`
and `jq` are available, inspect it with:

```sh
bundle_id="$(
  plistutil -i build-release/MyApp.app/Info.plist -f json -o - |
    jq -er '.CFBundleIdentifier'
)"
```

Replace `MyApp` with the actual application name and reject an empty or invalid
result. After the selected installer succeeds, allow a short bounded interval
for Activator to observe the newly registered application. Confirm that the
bundle identifier appears as an exact listener name:

```sh
activator listeners | grep -Fqx -- "$bundle_id"
```

Retry this read-only check for no more than a few seconds. If the listener still
does not appear, stop and report that application registration is incomplete.
Do not automatically run `uicache`, respring SpringBoard, reinstall the IPA, or
switch installers. Ask the user before performing any such recovery step.

Before launching, inspect the current device mode:

```sh
activator current-mode
```

If the result is `lockscreen`, ask the user to unlock the device. Never
automatically dismiss or bypass the lock screen, disable a passcode, or invoke
a lock-screen listener merely to make a test launch succeed.

Launch the exact application listener:

```sh
activator send "$bundle_id"
```

Verify the result independently with short, bounded retries:

```sh
activator current-app
```

Confirm a foreground launch only when `activator current-app` equals the
expected bundle identifier exactly. Do not treat the absence of command output
or the Activator process exit status alone as proof that the application
launched. If another application remains in the foreground, report the launch
as unverified or failed and inspect device state and crash logs without
repeatedly relaunching it.

`uiopen` accepts a URL rather than a bundle identifier. Use it only when the
application intentionally declares a URL scheme and the requested test
requires opening that URL. Use Activator to launch an installed application by
bundle identifier.

## Change Discipline and Handoff

Keep edits surgical. Do not rewrite a functioning build system solely to match
the sample. Update tests or portable harnesses when shared C behavior changes.
Review the complete diff before finishing and make sure only intended files
changed.

Report:

- what changed;
- the detected device architecture, selected SDK, and deployment target;
- the exact build, analyzer, packaging, and optional installation commands run;
- whether compiler and analyzer diagnostics were zero;
- the paths and structures of the resulting `.app` and IPA;
- anything not verified because a tool, SDK, library, permission, or runtime
  capability was unavailable; and
- the exact user action required for any missing package or privileged SDK
  operation.

Never claim a build, analysis, package inspection, install, or launch succeeded
unless its command actually completed successfully.

skills.title: macOS Development
skills.description: Build, inspect, repair, analyze, package, and optionally run native Objective-C and C applications locally on Mac OS X or macOS using only the SDKs, compilers, libraries, and package-manager tools already installed by the user. Use this skill for AppKit applications, legacy Cocoa compatibility, native-architecture Makefiles, `.app` bundles, and portable C shared with Cocoa code.
skills.instructions:
## Operating Principles

Inspect the project before changing it. Read every applicable `AGENTS.md`, the
existing Makefile or Xcode project, `Info.plist`, nearby source, and relevant
tests or harnesses. Preserve established project conventions unless the user
explicitly asks to change them.

Assume compilation happens locally on the Mac. Use only developer tools, SDKs,
frameworks, and libraries already installed by the user, including Xcode,
Command Line Tools, Homebrew, or MacPorts. Do not assume access to the Altivec
Intelligence container, `/altivec`, `/osxcross`, Docker, or a remote build host.

If another compiler, SDK, library, package, or command is required, explain
what is missing and ask the user to install it. Do not run `brew install`,
`port install`, an Xcode installer, `softwareupdate`, or any privileged package
operation yourself.

Make small, focused changes. Preserve unrelated work. Never commit or push.
Do not copy an app into `/Applications`, alter a system framework, change the
active developer directory, sign for distribution, or launch an app unless the
task and user authorization require it.

## Environment Discovery

Before designing or changing a build, inspect the local environment with
read-only commands such as:

```sh
uname -a
uname -m
sw_vers
id
pwd
command -v xcrun
command -v clang
command -v gcc
command -v cc
command -v make
command -v xcodebuild
command -v brew
command -v port
xcode-select -p 2>/dev/null || true
xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path 2>/dev/null || true
xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-version 2>/dev/null || true
```

Also inspect the project rather than assuming a template layout:

```sh
find . -name AGENTS.md -print
sed -n '1,260p' Makefile
ls -la
for directory in source/shared source/iOS source/macOS source/linux; do
  test ! -d "$directory" || find "$directory" -type f -print
done
```

Read `Info.plist` at its actual project path. If the project uses Xcode, inspect
its checked-in settings with read-only commands; do not rewrite it into a
Makefile merely because this skill contains a Makefile example.

Keep discovery bounded to the project and known developer-tool locations. Do
not scan the entire startup disk. Treat command presence as evidence only that
a command exists; confirm its version, target support, and selected SDK before
relying on it. On Apple Silicon, determine whether the shell is translated
before making architecture assumptions.

## SDK Configuration

Use only an installed macOS SDK. Prefer the SDK selected by the existing
project. For a new Makefile on a system with `xcrun`, discover it rather than
hard-coding an Xcode version:

```sh
xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path
xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-version
xcrun --sdk macosx --find clang
```

On an older Mac where `xcrun` does not exist, inspect the existing compiler and
project paths. Older Xcode releases may keep SDKs under `/Developer/SDKs` or an
Xcode platform directory, but never assume one of those locations without
checking it. Native compilation against the installed system frameworks may
not need an explicit `-isysroot`.

If no suitable SDK or compiler is installed, stop and ask the user to install
the appropriate Xcode or Command Line Tools version. Do not download an SDK,
copy one from another Mac, switch `xcode-select`, or patch SDK headers.

Treat SDK version and deployment target as separate settings. `SDKROOT`
controls compile-time headers and linker inputs. `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` or
`-mmacosx-version-min` controls the oldest runtime. Keep the Makefile,
`LSMinimumSystemVersion`, and actual API usage consistent. A new SDK does not
make a new selector safe on an old runtime.

When targeting Tiger, Leopard, or another legacy release, validate API names
against an installed SDK appropriate for that compatibility floor. If the
needed old SDK is not installed, report that limitation instead of claiming
legacy compatibility from a modern-only build.

## Architecture and Deployment Target

Build only for the architecture of the Mac on which the coding agent is
running. Normally, let the native compiler choose its default architecture.
Do not create a universal binary, invoke `lipo -create`, cross-compile PPC or
Intel from Apple Silicon, or build ARM from Intel merely because a compiler
accepts an `-arch` flag.

Use `uname -m`, compiler version output, and the final `file` result together.
If the shell is running under Rosetta, distinguish the process architecture
from the physical CPU and follow the user's actual target requirement. Do not
silently switch execution modes.

Choose the deployment target from the existing project requirement and the
host/runtime the user intends to support. If no target is documented, ask
before making a choice that changes API or language availability. Before using
an API newer than the target, use an established compatibility wrapper with a
safe runtime fallback or ask the user to raise the target.

## Project Structure

For a new cross-platform Cocoa application, prefer a source tree such as:

```text
MyApp/
  AGENTS.md                         optional project-specific guidance
  source/
    shared/                         code and resources used by both targets
      app_model.h
      app_model.c                   portable business logic
      Resources/
        en.lproj/
          Localizable.strings
    iOS/                            optional sibling mobile target
      Makefile
      Info.plist
      UI/
      Bridge/
      Resources/
      build-release/                generated iOS app bundle and IPA
      build-analyze/                generated Clang analyzer report
    macOS/
      Makefile                      run macOS make commands from this directory
      Info.plist
      main.m
      AppDelegate.h
      AppDelegate.m
      UI/                           AppKit controllers and views
      Bridge/                       macOS Objective-C/C adapters
      Resources/
        AppIcon.icns
      build-release/                generated MyApp.app
      build-analyze/                generated Clang analyzer report
    linux/                          optional portable-C tests or harnesses
```

Keep AppKit code in the platform UI layer. Keep networking policy, parsing,
database work, computation, and reusable business logic in portable C when
practical. Use a small, named bridge layer to convert between Cocoa objects and
C types. Put only genuinely cross-platform files under `source/shared`; never
put AppKit or UIKit imports in ordinary shared C files. Do not reorganize an
existing project merely to match this example.

Keep generated output beside the Makefile that owns it. With the layout above,
the macOS release path is `source/macOS/build-release/MyApp.app`. Do not create
a shared `source/build-release` directory unless the existing top-level build
system explicitly owns that path. Keep all build and analyzer directories
ignored by version control.

## Makefile Configuration

Place the macOS Makefile in `source/macOS` and run its commands from that
directory. Resolve `../shared` relative to that location. Reuse a functioning
Makefile when one exists. For a new native application, use a small Makefile
that discovers installed tools, enables warnings, builds only the native
architecture, runs Clang analysis when available, and creates a real app
bundle. For example:

```makefile
APP_NAME := MyApp
BUILD_DIR := build-release
OBJECT_DIR := $(BUILD_DIR)/Intermediates
APP_BUNDLE := $(BUILD_DIR)/$(APP_NAME).app
EXECUTABLE := $(APP_BUNDLE)/Contents/MacOS/$(APP_NAME)
INFO_PLIST := Info.plist
RESOURCE_DIR := Resources
SHARED_RESOURCE_DIR := ../shared/Resources

OBJC_SOURCES := main.m AppDelegate.m UI/MainWindowController.m \
	Bridge/AppModelBridge.m
C_SOURCES := ../shared/app_model.c
OBJC_OBJECTS := $(patsubst %.m,$(OBJECT_DIR)/%.o,$(OBJC_SOURCES))
C_OBJECTS := $(patsubst ../shared/%.c,$(OBJECT_DIR)/shared/%.o,$(C_SOURCES))
OBJECTS := $(OBJC_OBJECTS) $(C_OBJECTS)

CLANG := $(shell command -v clang 2>/dev/null)
CC := $(if $(CLANG),$(CLANG),cc)
SDKROOT := $(shell xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path 2>/dev/null)
SDK_FLAGS := $(if $(strip $(SDKROOT)),-isysroot "$(SDKROOT)")

WARNINGS := -Wall -Wextra -Werror
CPPFLAGS := -I../shared
CFLAGS := -std=c99 -O2 $(WARNINGS)
OBJCFLAGS := -std=c99 -O2 $(WARNINGS)
FRAMEWORKS := -framework Cocoa

.DEFAULT_GOAL := release
.PHONY: release analyze clean

release: analyze $(APP_BUNDLE)

$(APP_BUNDLE): $(EXECUTABLE) $(INFO_PLIST)
	@mkdir -p "$@/Contents/Resources"
	@cp "$(INFO_PLIST)" "$@/Contents/Info.plist"
	@if test -d "$(SHARED_RESOURCE_DIR)"; then \
		cp -R "$(SHARED_RESOURCE_DIR)/." "$@/Contents/Resources/"; \
	fi
	@if test -d "$(RESOURCE_DIR)"; then \
		cp -R "$(RESOURCE_DIR)/." "$@/Contents/Resources/"; \
	fi
	@printf 'APPL????' > "$@/Contents/PkgInfo"

$(EXECUTABLE): $(OBJECTS)
	@mkdir -p "$(@D)"
	$(CC) $(SDK_FLAGS) $(OBJECTS) $(LDFLAGS) $(FRAMEWORKS) $(LDLIBS) -o "$@"

$(OBJECT_DIR)/%.o: %.m
	@mkdir -p "$(@D)"
	$(CC) $(CPPFLAGS) $(SDK_FLAGS) $(OBJCFLAGS) -c "$<" -o "$@"

$(OBJECT_DIR)/%.o: %.c
	@mkdir -p "$(@D)"
	$(CC) $(CPPFLAGS) $(SDK_FLAGS) $(CFLAGS) -c "$<" -o "$@"

$(OBJECT_DIR)/shared/%.o: ../shared/%.c
	@mkdir -p "$(@D)"
	$(CC) $(CPPFLAGS) $(SDK_FLAGS) $(CFLAGS) -c "$<" -o "$@"

analyze:
	@if test -n "$(CLANG)"; then \
		mkdir -p build-analyze; \
		: > build-analyze/analyze.txt; \
		for source in $(OBJC_SOURCES); do \
			"$(CLANG)" $(CPPFLAGS) $(SDK_FLAGS) $(OBJCFLAGS) --analyze \
				"$$source" >> build-analyze/analyze.txt 2>&1 || exit $$?; \
		done; \
		for source in $(C_SOURCES); do \
			"$(CLANG)" $(CPPFLAGS) $(SDK_FLAGS) $(CFLAGS) --analyze \
				"$$source" >> build-analyze/analyze.txt 2>&1 || exit $$?; \
		done; \
		cat build-analyze/analyze.txt; \
	else \
		printf '%s\n' 'Clang is unavailable; static analysis was not run.'; \
	fi

clean:
	rm -rf build-release build-analyze
```

The example copies shared resources first and macOS-specific resources second.
Avoid duplicate relative paths rather than relying on that order to overwrite
one resource with another. Keep platform icons and AppKit-only nibs under
`source/macOS/Resources`; keep common localizations, JSON, HTML, fonts, and
other genuinely shared runtime data under `source/shared/Resources`. Every
resource directory must be copied explicitly into `Contents/Resources`.

Treat this as a starting point, not a replacement for project evidence. Add a
confirmed `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, dependency flags, ARC/MRC flags, nibs,
localizations, signing, or packaging only when the project needs them.

Keep `-Wall` enabled whether the selected compiler is GCC or Clang. Add
`-Wextra` and other supported warnings. Fix every warning; do not remove useful
warning flags or suppress a category globally to make the build green. If an
old API is intentionally required, isolate a narrowly scoped deprecation
suppression inside the compatibility implementation and document its fallback.

Every Makefile must provide `make release` and `make clean`. When Clang is
available, it must provide and use `make analyze`. `make release` must create a
properly structured `.app`; `make clean` must remove only known generated build
and analysis directories, never source, resources, installed libraries, or user
data.

## Application Bundle and Package Structure

A macOS application bundle must use the `Contents` hierarchy:

```text
build-release/
  MyApp.app/
    Contents/
      Info.plist
      PkgInfo                  optional legacy metadata
      MacOS/
        MyApp                  native Mach-O executable
      Resources/
        AppIcon.icns
        en.lproj/
          Localizable.strings
      Frameworks/              embedded private frameworks or dylibs, if used
      PlugIns/                 application plug-ins, if used
      _CodeSignature/          present only after code signing
```

Keep `CFBundleExecutable` equal to the executable name. Put ordinary resources,
icons, nibs, and localizations under `Contents/Resources`. Put private dynamic
frameworks and bundled dylibs under `Contents/Frameworks` only after fixing and
verifying their loader paths. Do not use the flat iOS bundle layout and do not
put the executable at the `.app` root.

If distribution requires a ZIP, preserve symlinks inside versioned frameworks.
Do not confuse a ZIP, disk image, installer package, or copied `.app` with the
app bundle itself.

## Info.plist and Resources

Require a project-owned `Info.plist`. At minimum, verify coherent values for:

- `CFBundleExecutable`
- `CFBundleIdentifier`
- `CFBundleName` or `CFBundleDisplayName`
- `CFBundlePackageType` (`APPL`)
- `CFBundleShortVersionString`
- `CFBundleVersion`
- `LSMinimumSystemVersion` when a deployment floor is declared
- `CFBundleIconFile` when the app includes an icon

Add only document types, URL schemes, services, privacy descriptions,
principal-class settings, nib names, or capabilities the app actually needs.
Do not fabricate a bundle identifier, version, signing identity, entitlement,
or deployment floor. Ask the user when those are product decisions.

Preserve `.lproj` directories and other resource subdirectories. Legacy Cocoa
may expect `.strings` files in a particular encoding; follow the existing
project and target requirements rather than blindly transcoding them. Verify
that every declared resource exists before packaging.

Keep the application icon under `source/macOS/Resources` as an `.icns` file and
make `CFBundleIconFile` match its bundled filename. Do not substitute iOS PNG
icons for the Mac icon. Put nibs, help content, and AppKit-only images in the
same platform resource tree.

Store localized resources in language-specific directories such as:

```text
source/shared/Resources/
  en.lproj/
    Localizable.strings
    InfoPlist.strings        optional localized bundle metadata
  ja.lproj/
    Localizable.strings
    InfoPlist.strings
```

Copy each `.lproj` directory intact into `MyApp.app/Contents/Resources`. Use
`NSLocalizedString` or the project's established localization API instead of
hard-coded user-facing strings. Validate that every supported locale contains
the required keys. When a legacy target requires UTF-16 `.strings` files,
transcode only in the build output; keep the source-of-truth files in the
project's documented encoding.

## Coding Style

Never use Swift. Write Objective-C for Cocoa/UI integration and C for portable
logic. Do not introduce Objective-C++ unless an existing dependency requires
it and the project already supports it.

Use bracketed Objective-C message syntax. Do not use dot syntax, even when the
compiler accepts a property:

```objective-c
[[window contentView] setNeedsDisplay:YES];
title = [document displayName];
```

Do not write:

```objective-c
window.contentView.needsDisplay = YES;
title = document.displayName;
```

Match the existing indentation and naming conventions. In a new project,
prefer 2-space indentation, no tabs in source, readable lower-camel-case method
names, trailing underscores for private instance variables, and prefixed public
C symbols. Use `YES` and `NO` for `BOOL`. Never retain a delegate.

For Tiger, Leopard, or another Objective-C 1.0-era compatibility target, avoid
ARC, blocks, property declarations, synthesized accessors, class extensions,
object literals, subscripting, `instancetype`, zeroing weak references, and
other Objective-C 2.0 or modern-language conventions. Use declared instance
variables, manual accessors, `NSAutoreleasePool`, delegates/selectors, and
ordinary collection methods. For a newer target, still follow the existing
project's language and memory-management style.

Avoid premature optimization, but prefer pure C for hot computation, parsers,
database adapters, networking engines, and reusable business rules when it
improves portability or performance. Keep window/view lifecycle, AppKit event
handling, and conversion to display objects in Objective-C.

## C and Objective-C Boundaries

Keep ordinary `.c` files platform-neutral. Do not include AppKit, Foundation,
CoreFoundation, Objective-C runtime, or other Apple-framework headers from C.
Use standard C headers and project-owned portable headers. Do not make a C
header expose `NSString`, `NSArray`, `NSData`, Objective-C `id`, `NSView`, or
other Cocoa types.

Do not let every Objective-C file import the C model and third-party C
libraries. Designate narrow bridge `.m` files that are allowed to include both
sides. Expose Objective-C methods to the UI and portable C functions to the C
core. Convert strings, byte buffers, ownership, errors, and callbacks at that
boundary.

Objective-C may include narrow system C headers when Cocoa has no suitable
surface, but keep those uses local. Import project C headers, `curl/curl.h`,
`sqlite3.h`, and `cJSON.h` only in designated model or bridge implementations.
Never pass a `cJSON *`, `sqlite3 *`, or libcurl handle into a view controller.

Keep C libraries in C until data must cross into AppKit. Parse responses,
execute SQL, and transform cJSON trees in C. Bridge only the final model or
presentation values needed by the UI. Make ownership explicit on both sides.

## Memory Management and Runtime Compatibility

Inspect the deployment target, compiler flags, and existing files before
choosing ARC or MRC. Legacy Mac OS X targets do not support ARC and may not
support blocks or other modern Objective-C runtime features. Never enable ARC
for a translation unit that contains manual ownership calls or must build for a
legacy runtime.

For MRC code:

- Balance every owned object with `release` or `autorelease`.
- Release owned instance variables in `dealloc`, then call `[super dealloc]`.
- Implement explicit getters and setters when properties are unavailable.
- Copy strings or mutable-value inputs when the object must retain a stable
  value.
- Never retain delegates or other documented back-pointers.
- Use `NSAutoreleasePool` instead of `@autoreleasepool` when required.

For modern ARC-only code, do not add manual ownership messages. Keep MRC shared
files separate and compile each translation unit with the correct flags.

Centralize compatibility logic in a small layer, commonly named
`XPFoundation` or `XPAppKit`. At feature call sites, use the wrapper instead of
repeating SDK checks. Use compile-time checks only for declarations the
compiler must parse. Use `respondsToSelector:` before invoking an optional
runtime method and provide an oldest-runtime fallback. Follow the project's
established invocation pattern; object-only selectors may use
`performSelector:`, while primitive or struct arguments/returns require a typed
and signature-safe mechanism such as `NSInvocation`.

When a formal protocol or constant is absent from an old SDK, hide the
compile-time difference behind a compatibility protocol, macro, category, or
typedef. Keep deprecation pragmas inside that compatibility implementation, not
throughout feature code. A warning-free modern build does not prove that a
selector exists on an old system, so test the actual legacy runtime whenever it
is available.

## AltivecToolchain

Do not assume the Altivec Intelligence container or its `/altivec` and
`/osxcross` paths exist on macOS. The on-device `AltivecToolchain` Debian
package is an iOS environment and is not a substitute for Xcode or Command Line
Tools on a Mac. Use an Altivec-provided Mac library or Make include only when
the current project or user has actually installed it and the exact path is
present.

For a normal local Mac build, obtain compiler and SDK paths from the installed
Xcode toolchain. Obtain modern libcurl, SQLite, and cJSON headers/libraries only
from locations already installed by the user, such as a verified Homebrew or
MacPorts prefix, or from dependencies already checked into the project. Do not
copy container paths into a local Makefile.

Before linking a dependency, confirm its exact header, archive or dylib,
architecture, deployment compatibility, and transitive libraries. The presence
of a `curl` or `sqlite3` executable does not prove that matching development
headers and linkable libraries exist.

If a required dependency is absent, ask the user to install it. State the
dependency and why it is required, but let the user choose Xcode, Homebrew,
MacPorts, or another approved source. Reinspect the installed prefix afterward;
do not assume a package manager's default prefix or formula layout.

## Third-Party Libraries

Prefer an already-established project dependency configuration. When
`pkg-config` is installed and the relevant `.pc` files exist, use its reported
flags rather than guessing transitive link dependencies. Otherwise, inspect
verified prefixes, for example:

```makefile
# Set these only to paths confirmed on this Mac.
CURL_PREFIX := /confirmed/curl/prefix
SQLITE_PREFIX := /confirmed/sqlite/prefix
CJSON_PREFIX := /confirmed/cjson/prefix

CPPFLAGS += -I$(CURL_PREFIX)/include \
	-I$(SQLITE_PREFIX)/include \
	-I$(CJSON_PREFIX)/include
LDFLAGS += -L$(CURL_PREFIX)/lib \
	-L$(SQLITE_PREFIX)/lib \
	-L$(CJSON_PREFIX)/lib
LDLIBS += -lcurl -lsqlite3 -lcjson
```

Treat every `/confirmed/...` value as a placeholder. Do not paste it literally.
Confirm the actual cJSON library spelling and libcurl's private dependencies.
Do not mix headers from Homebrew with libraries from MacPorts or the system.

Prefer static linkage when it is available for the native architecture and
deployment target and produces a self-contained legacy-compatible app. If
dynamic linkage is required, copy non-system dylibs into
`Contents/Frameworks`, rewrite their install names to a bundle-relative form
supported by the target OS, and verify the complete dependency graph with
`otool -L`. Do not embed Apple system frameworks.

Keep libcurl operations in a C networking module, SQLite work in a C storage
module, and cJSON work in C model/protocol modules. Check every return code,
bound inputs, use prepared SQL statements, free every resource on all paths,
set network timeouts, and preserve TLS peer and host verification. Bundle the
CA certificate source expected by the chosen libcurl build when necessary.

## Build, Analysis, and Verification

After source or build changes, run a clean analysis and release build while
capturing the complete output:

```sh
make clean
make analyze
make release
```

If the existing project uses different documented commands, run their exact
equivalents while preserving `release` and `clean` entry points. Do not truncate
output with `tail`. Keep temporary logs outside committed resources and do not
commit generated logs, bundles, objects, dependency files, analyzer reports,
or archives unless the user explicitly asks.

Require zero compiler warnings and zero analyzer diagnostics. If Clang is
installed, run its static analyzer over every affected C and Objective-C
source. An empty analyzer report may mean the analysis is clean; confirm the
command completed and covered the expected sources. If only GCC is available,
report that Clang analysis could not run rather than claiming equivalent
coverage.

Verify the bundle with available local tools:

```sh
test -d build-release/MyApp.app
test -x build-release/MyApp.app/Contents/MacOS/MyApp
file build-release/MyApp.app/Contents/MacOS/MyApp
otool -L build-release/MyApp.app/Contents/MacOS/MyApp
plutil -lint build-release/MyApp.app/Contents/Info.plist
find build-release/MyApp.app -print
```

Replace `MyApp` with the actual `APP_NAME`. Confirm the executable has only the
intended native architecture, the bundle layout is correct, resources are
present, and every non-system dynamic dependency resolves from the bundle or a
documented installed location. Validate behavior on the oldest promised Mac OS
X runtime whenever that machine is available; a successful build on a new Mac
is not sufficient evidence of legacy runtime compatibility.

## Installation and Execution

A macOS `.app` can normally run directly from `build-release`; copying it to
`/Applications` is not part of compilation. Launch or execute it only when the
user asks or project instructions explicitly require a safe smoke test. Before
launching, inspect its target, dependencies, configuration, and expected data
locations.

Do not copy over an installed app, kill an existing process, remove quarantine,
bypass Gatekeeper, alter ownership, or clear preferences without explicit user
approval. Do not ad-hoc sign, apply entitlements, notarize, or create an
installer unless requested. Signing and notarization require user-owned
identity and product decisions; never invent them.

For a permitted smoke test, capture standard output and error when possible and
check for uncaught exceptions, missing selectors, missing dylibs, and immediate
termination. Report when the current Mac cannot run the chosen deployment
target or architecture.

## Change Discipline and Handoff

Keep edits surgical. Do not rewrite a functioning build system solely to match
the sample. Update tests or portable harnesses when shared C behavior changes.
Review the complete diff before finishing and make sure only intended files
changed.

Report:

- what changed;
- the detected Mac/process architecture, selected SDK, and deployment target;
- the exact build, analyzer, bundle-validation, and optional launch commands;
- whether compiler and analyzer diagnostics were zero;
- the path and verified structure of the resulting `.app`;
- any unverified legacy-runtime, signing, dependency, or launch behavior; and
- the exact tool, SDK, or library the user must install when the local
  environment is incomplete.

Never claim a build, analysis, bundle inspection, signing step, or launch
succeeded unless its command actually completed successfully.
